Recommendations
REC-01

Computer vision on the assembly line

Start short-term

Use the CCTV feeds you already have to measure cycle time, value-added vs idle time, and process adherence per station — then build toward lights-out / dark-factory cells over the long run.

Why now: the cameras and footage already exist. Annotate that video and you get worker-level efficiency data with almost no new hardware.

REF · BMW runs camera + AI quality/efficiency checks (AIQX) across every plant.  View case study →
REC-02

VR + haptics training for new operators

Cuts scrap

Train assembly and machining skills in VR with force-feedback gloves — operators feel torque and tension on a virtual job, so no raw material or live line is consumed during training.

The company you mentioned: SenseGlove (Delft, NL) — force-feedback gloves already used by Volkswagen, Fraunhofer and the Dutch defence forces.

REF · SenseGlove Nova — 20 N feedback per finger.  senseglove.com →
REC-03

Digital twins of machines & lines

Simulate first

Build a live virtual replica of a machine or cell to simulate changes, test process tweaks and predict wear before touching the physical asset.

Fit for Parason: with metallurgy, design and build all in-house, you own every input a twin needs — a rare advantage.

REF · BMW modelled its Debrecen plant as a full digital twin before building it.  Read more →

Recommendation 01 — Computer vision
REC-01

Vision analytics on the assembly line

Put computer vision on the assembly cells to read the line the way an industrial engineer would — but continuously and per operator. The goal is data labelling of work: each station's cycle time, the split between value-added and idle/non-value time, and whether the "golden" sequence is followed every cycle.

Short termUse existing CCTV. The cameras and footage are already there. Annotate that video to track operator timelines, efficiency and bottlenecks — minimal new hardware, fast to pilot on one line.
Long termLights-out / dark cells. The dark-lab idea from our earlier call — machines running unmanned with no need for human lighting or comfort load — is the natural endpoint once the vision layer and automation mature.
Case studyBMW's AIQX platform runs camera- and sensor-based AI checks across every BMW plant; European plants have reported sizeable defect-rate reductions. Dedicated tools like Drishti / Retrocausal do exactly the operator motion + cycle-time analysis from video. automotivemanufacturingsolutions.com
NoteWorker-monitoring works best framed as process improvement and training, with the team in the loop — that's how these deployments hold up on the floor.
Recommendation 02 — VR + haptics training
REC-02

Industry-4.0 training without scrap

New operators learning on a live line cost material and time. Move first-stage training into VR with haptic force-feedback gloves: a trainee tightening a fastener or assembling a component feels the real torque and tension virtually, builds the muscle memory, and consumes zero raw material or line time.

VendorSenseGlove (Delft, Netherlands) — the company you were thinking of. Their Nova glove delivers up to 20 N of force feedback per finger via magnetic friction brakes. senseglove.com
In use byVolkswagen (VR assembly training), Fraunhofer and University of Cambridge (research), and the Royal Netherlands Army for assembling complex machinery — a close analogue to your work.
Worth comparingHaptX and Dexmo make higher-end force-feedback gloves; worth a quick benchmark on price vs realism before committing.
PayoffLess scrap during onboarding, faster ramp-up, and safe rehearsal of hazardous or high-precision steps.
Recommendation 03 — Digital twins
REC-03

Simulate before you build

Create digital twins of key machines and lines — live virtual replicas fed by sensor data — to simulate process changes, predict wear and failures, and validate a redesign before any metal is cut or a line is stopped.

Why ParasonA twin is only as good as the engineering data behind it. With foundry, metallurgy, design and assembly all in-house, you already own every input — material properties, geometry, process parameters — that most firms have to source externally.
Case studyBMW built a complete digital twin of its Debrecen plant before a single component was installed. Platforms such as Siemens and NVIDIA Omniverse are the common toolchains. Reference
Where to startTwin one high-value asset first — e.g. a refiner or a key lathe cell — prove the value, then widen.

Shop-floor automation — to be detailed by our team

Smaller efficiency changes spotted around the basket / machining area. Pointers for now; full notes to follow.
  • Chip management — add chip breakers to raise tool life, plus a conveyor to auto-collect chips and keep cells clean
  • Welding — a radially-rotating automated welder that indexes around the job for fixed, repeatable welds
  • Basket ring — evaluate alternatives to the current laser-cut method
  • Basket build — automate the assembly sequence and surrounding handling
